works.abstract: ABSTRACT Dicarboxylic acids are key components of many polymers and plastics, making them a target for both engineered microbial degradation and sustainable bioproduction. In this study, we generated a comprehensive data set of functional evidence for the genetic basis of dicarboxylic and fatty acid metabolism using randomly barcoded transposon sequencing (RB-TnSeq). We identified four β-proteobacteria that displayed robust growth with dicarboxylic acid sole carbon source and cultured their mutant libraries with dicarboxylic and fatty acids with carbon chain lengths from C3 to C12. The resulting fitness data suggested that dicarboxylic and fatty acid metabolisms are largely distinct, and different sets of β-oxidation genes are required for catabolizing dicarboxylic versus fatty acids of the same carbon chain lengths. In addition, we identified transcriptional regulators and transporters with strong fitness phenotypes related to dicarboxylic acid utilization. In Ralstonia sp . UNC404CL21Col ( R. CL21 ), we deleted two transcriptional repressors to improve its utilization of short-chain dicarboxylic acids. We exploited the diacid-utilizing catabolism of R. CL21 to upcycle a mock mixture of the dicarboxylic acids produced when polyethylene is oxidized. After introducing a heterologous indigoidine production pathway, this engineered Ralstonia produced 0.56 ± 0.02 g/L indigoidine from a mixture of dicarboxylic acids as a carbon source, demonstrating the potential of R. CL21 to upcycle plastic wastes to products derived from tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle intermediates. IMPORTANCE Upcycling the carbon in plastic wastes to value-added products is a promising approach to address the plastic waste and climate crises, and dicarboxylic acid metabolism is an important facet of several approaches. Improving our understanding of the genetic basis of this metabolism has the potential to uncover new enzymes and genetic parts for engineered pathways involving dicarboxylic acids. Our data set is the most comprehensive interrogation of dicarboxylic acid catabolism to date, and this work will be of utility to researchers interested in both plastics bioproduction and upcycling applications.
works.title: RB-TnSeq elucidates dicarboxylic-acid-specific catabolism in β-proteobacteria for improved plastic monomer upcycling

works.abstract: Microbes possess diverse natural metabolisms, both in the carbon sources they are capable of utilizing and the chemicals that they naturally produce. These metabolisms provide a rich source of tools that can be leveraged to address global environmental problems through the upcycling of diverse and renewable carbon sources into value-added products. The focus of this dissertation is the characterization of the genetic basis of microbial metabolisms, answering foundational questions about metabolism and its regulation, but with the potential for applications in metabolic engineering and synthetic biology in mind.Randomly barcoded transposon sequencing (RB-TnSeq) allows rapid genome-wide profiling of individual gene fitness under a selective condition in a high-throughput manner. In this method, a library of transposon mutants – each carrying a DNA barcode that is mapped to the gene it disrupts – is created. This library is exposed to a selective condition that will result in the enrichment or depletion of barcoded mutants, depending on whether disruption of each gene was beneficial, neutral, or detrimental in the selective condition. The fitness data generated in this approach can provide strong evidence for both individual gene functions and broader metabolic pathways.Chapter 1 discusses the characterization of the genetic basis of fatty acid, alcohol, and nitrogen metabolism in the metabolic engineering workhorse P. putida using RB-TnSeq. Functional evidence for metabolic predictions based on homology is generated, and previously uncharacterized metabolisms are posited. Many of the tested compounds have industrial relevance for the biofuel, polymer, and food industries, and the data should be of use in engineered bioproduction efforts.In Chapter 2, RB-TnSeq is then applied to less-studied, environmental isolates capable of metabolizing dicarboxylic acids, which are relevant in plastics and polymers applications. Genes responsible for dicarboxylic acid β-oxidation, transport, and regulation are identified, and found to be largely distinct from those involved in fatty acid metabolism. These data will be useful to metabolic engineers aiming to both engineer the production and degradation of dicarboxylic acids. The chapter also explores the potential of one of these organisms, Ralstonia sp. UNC404CL21Col, as a non-model host for plastic upcycling and provides a proof-of-concept demonstration.Finally, Chapter 3 focuses on gene regulation, beginning with the characterization of tools for heterologous expression based on well-established regulators. Next, the influence of regulator specificity on the apparent genetic basis of nitrogenous compound metabolism is examined, and new regulators with potential utility in engineered pathways are identified. Finally, guided by publicly available fitness data, AraC/XylS family regulators from P. putida are characterized, confirming regulators with known functions, characterizing regulators with predicted functions, and identifying a novel regulator.Altogether, this work explores the genetic basis of metabolism and its regulation in one model and four non-model organisms, one of which is further developed as an engineering chassis. Pathways that are important for engineering these microbes are characterized, and the genes uncovered could also have relevance in engineering other organisms. Regulation of this metabolism is also considered, and this knowledge is leveraged to create new regulatory tools. While a general understanding of metabolic pathways is beneficial for engineering, a focus on chemicals with industrial significance makes this work particularly useful for efforts to engineer microbial cell factories for more sustainable, environmentally-friendly bioproduction.
works.title: Characterizing microbial metabolism and its regulation to enable sustainable bioproduction
